title: Duration as a tangent line
objectives: Approximate a bond’s price change with its first derivative.
Compute modified duration and DV01, and say when they mislead

screens.title: Price against yield
screens.prose: A 5-year bond pays a £4 coupon each year and £100 at the end. At a 5% yield its price is £95.67. The curve is its price at every yield, and the dashed line is the tangent at 5%. Move the yield and compare them.
screens.question: Move the yield from 5% to 6%. By about how much does the price fall?

widget.label: Fall in price
widget.accept: about £4.10: from £95.67 to £91.58. The tangent says £4.21.

hints.text: Read the price at 5%, then at 6%.

feedback.correct: About £4.09. The tangent says £4.21, close for a 1-point move.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the price at 5% and at 6%, and subtract.

byKey.one-pct: You took 1% off the price. This bond loses about 4% of its value when its yield rises 1 point.
byKey.sign: A fall is a positive amount here. The price drops from £95.67 to about £91.58.

explain.text: The price falls from £95.67 to £91.58, about £4.09. The tangent predicts £4.21, close for a 1-point move. The curve bends up, so the line sits a little below it.

screens.title: The slope
screens.prose: The tangent's slope is $P'(y)$. Each cash flow $c_t (1+y)^{-t}$ differentiates by the chain rule to $-t\,c_t (1+y)^{-t-1}$. The table lists the sizes $t\,c_t / 1.05^{t+1}$.
screens.question: Fill in the year-5 term and the total.

hints.text: Year 5 pays the last coupon and the face: £104.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $520 / 1.05^6$, then add the five terms.

explain.text: The year-5 term is $520 / 1.05^6 = 388.03$, and the total is 420.98. So $P'(0.05) = -420.98$ pounds per unit of yield. The final payment dominates: it is large and far away.

screens.title: Per pound held
screens.prose: The slope $-420.98$ is in pounds per unit of yield, for a price of £95.67. Divide by the price to get the fractional change per unit of yield.
screens.question: Compute $-P'(0.05) / P(0.05)$.

byKey.sign: You kept the minus sign. $P'$ is negative, and the extra minus makes the result positive.
byKey.inverted: You divided the price by the slope. Put $-P'$ on top.
byKey.no-price: That is the slope alone. Divide it by the price, £95.67.

explain.text: $420.98 / 95.6705 = 4.40$. This number is the bond's **modified duration**, $D = -P'(y)/P(y)$. The price falls about 4.40% for each 1-point rise in yield.

screens.prose: The **modified duration** is $D = -P'/P = 4.40$. Along the tangent, a yield change $\Delta y$ moves the price by $P'\,\Delta y = -D\,P\,\Delta y$.
screens.question: Yields rise from 5% to 6%. By how much does the tangent say the price falls?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $D$, $\Delta y = 0.01$ and the price.

byKey.no-price: You found $D \times 0.01 = 0.044$, the fractional fall. Multiply by the price, £95.67.
byKey.face: You applied 4.40% to the £100 face. Duration works on today's price, £95.67.
byKey.units: You used $\Delta y = 1$. One percentage point is $\Delta y = 0.01$.

explain.text: $4.4003 \times 0.01 \times 95.6705 = 4.21$. The tangent's price at 6% is $95.67 - 4.21 = \text{£}91.46$. The true price is £91.58.

screens.title: Tangent against truth
screens.prose: At 6% the true price is £91.58, and the tangent says £91.46. The view is zoomed in around 6%.
screens.question: How does the true price compare with the tangent's, and why?

options.text: £0.11 above: the price curve bends upwards

options.why: You read the subtraction the wrong way round. $91.58 - 91.46 = +0.11$: the curve is above the line.

options.text: Equal: the tangent is exact for a bond
options.why: The tangent is exact only at 5% itself. Away from it the curve bends away.
That is the predicted fall, not the gap between the two prices.

hints.text: Subtract the tangent's price from the true price.
Positive: the curve is above the line, so it bends up.

feedback.correct: The curve is £0.11 above the tangent.

byKey.below: You took the tangent's price from the true price the wrong way round. The true price is higher.

explain.text: The gap is $91.5753 - 91.4607 = \text{£}0.11$, with the curve above the line. A curve that bends up has $P'' > 0$, so the tangent underestimates, as in lesson 2. That bend is **convexity**, the subject of the next level.

screens.title: A big move
screens.prose: Rates jump 3 points, from 5% to 8%. The tangent was £0.11 out for a 1-point move. A colleague says for 3 points it will be about $3 \times 0.11 = \text{£}0.33$ out.
screens.question: About how far is the tangent from the true price at 8%?

hints.text: In lesson 2 the error grew with $h^2$.
Three times the move gives $3^2 = 9$ times the error.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The error grows with the square of the move.

byKey.linear: You scaled the error in step with the move. It grows with the square: 3 times the move, 9 times the error.
byKey.same: You kept the 1-point error. The gap widens as the move grows.
byKey.fall: That is the predicted fall, $4.40 \times 0.03 \times 95.67$. The question asks for the gap from the true price.

explain.text: The error grows with the square of the move: $9 \times 0.1145 = 1.03$. The tangent gives £83.04 and the true price is £84.03, a gap of £0.99. Duration alone is fine for small moves and poor for big ones.

screens.prose: You priced a yield change with the tangent at today's yield. For a small change $\Delta y$: $$\Delta P \approx P'(y)\,\Delta y = -D\,P\,\Delta y, \quad D = -\dfrac{P'(y)}{P(y)}$$ Yield up, price down.
screens.question: Duration 4.40, price £95.67, and yields fall 0.5%. What does the tangent give?

options.why: You kept the price falling. Yields fell, so $\Delta y = -0.005$ and $\Delta P$ is positive.
$4.40 \times 0.005 = 0.022$ is the fractional change. Multiply by the price.
That is for a 1-point move. Half a point gives half: £2.10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $\Delta y = -0.005$ into $-D\,P\,\Delta y$.

explain.text: $\Delta P \approx -4.40 \times (-0.005) \times 95.67 = +2.10$. The two minus signs make a rise. The true price at 4.5% is £97.81, again a little above the line.

screens.prose: Where does $D$ come from? Write the price as a sum of cash flows $c_t$, where $c_T$ includes the face.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $P(y) = \sum_t c_t (1+y)^{-t}$, each cash flow discounted at yield $y$
$P'(y) = -\sum_t t\,c_t (1+y)^{-t-1}$, the chain rule on each $(1+y)^{-t}$
$\Delta P \approx -\sum_t t\,c_t (1+y)^{-t-1}\,\Delta y$, the tangent line with that slope

hints.text: Differentiate before you can use the slope.
Price, derivative, tangent, then divide by the price.

feedback.correct: Price, slope, tangent, then per pound.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need the derivative before the tangent can use it.

byKey.tangent: The tangent uses the slope, so the derivative comes first.
byKey.divide: Dividing by the price is the last step, once you have the tangent.

explain.text: Differentiating each discount factor gives the slope, and the tangent turns it into a price change. Dividing by $P$ makes it a fraction of the price. That fraction per unit of yield is $D$.

screens.title: DV01
screens.prose: Your book holds £10 million face of this bond, worth £9,567,052 at 5%. Risk is quoted as **DV01**: the pounds lost when the yield rises one basis point, 0.01%, or $\Delta y = 0.0001$.
screens.question: What is the position's DV01?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the duration, the market value and 0.0001.

byKey.face: You applied duration to the £10m face. Use the market value, £9,567,052.
byKey.per-point: That is for a full percentage point, 100 basis points. One basis point is $\Delta y = 0.0001$.
byKey.per-100: That is per £100 of face. Scale it up to the whole position.

explain.text: $4.4003 \times \text{£}9{,}567{,}052 \times 0.0001 = \text{£}4{,}209.80$. For a 1 bp move the tangent's error is tiny: the true loss is £4,208.63. That is why desks size hedges from DV01.

ideas: A bond's price-yield curve is smooth, so its tangent predicts small price changes.
Modified duration $D = -P'/P$ turns the slope into a fraction of the price. Yield up, price down.
The tangent underestimates the price for moves either way, and its error grows with the square of the move. That bend is convexity.

formula.name: Duration approximation
formula.note: $\Delta y$ in decimals: one basis point is 0.0001.

summary.trap: Duration is a tangent. It is fine for a few basis points and poor for a 3-point jump, where the error is nine times the 1-point error.

quiz.prose: A bond has modified duration 6.0 and price £102.00. Its yield falls by 0.25%.
quiz.question: What does the duration estimate give for the price change?

options.why: Yields fell, so the price rises. Yield and price move in opposite directions.
$6.0 \times 0.0025 = 0.015$ is the fractional change. Multiply by £102.
That is for a full 1-point fall. A quarter point gives a quarter of it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\Delta P \approx -D\,P\,\Delta y$ with $\Delta y = -0.0025$.

explain.text: $\Delta P \approx -6.0 \times 102 \times (-0.0025) = +1.53$. The yield fell, so the price rose.

quiz.prose: A bond is priced at £104.50, and the slope of its price-yield curve there is $P'(y) = -731.50$.
quiz.question: What is its modified duration?

explain.text: $D = -P'/P = 731.50 / 104.50 = 7.00$. The price falls about 7% per 1-point rise in yield.

quiz.prose: A bond position is worth £5,000,000 and has modified duration 3.2.
quiz.question: What is its DV01, in pounds per basis point?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply duration, value and $\Delta y = 0.0001$.

quiz.prose: The same bond, duration 4.40, faces four yield moves.
quiz.question: For which move is the duration estimate least reliable?

options.why: A tiny move: the tangent's error there is about a ten-thousandth of a 1-point error.
Still small. The error is about a hundredth of the 1-point error.
The error is a quarter of the 1-point error, about £0.03.

feedback.correct: The 2-point move: four times the 1-point error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The error grows with the square of the move.

explain.text: The tangent's error grows with $(\Delta y)^2$, whichever way the yield moves. A 2-point move leaves about four times the 1-point error: £0.49 here.
